n: This chapter summarizes David’s military victories, which fulfilled God’s promise to give Israel rest. First, David subdues the Philistines, Israel’s longtime oppressors.

f.g: Possibly “the bridle of the mother city” — control of the Philistines’ chief city. 1 Chronicles 18:1 says “Gath and her towns.”

n: David conquers Moab and executes two-thirds of its captured soldiers, measured by lines as they lay on the ground. It is a harsh practice of ancient warfare, recorded plainly. Moab becomes a tributary state.

f.g: David’s great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite, and he had once sheltered his parents there (1 Samuel 22:3-4), which makes this conflict striking.
Paid tribute — regular payments from a conquered nation.

n: David defeats Hadadezer, king of Zobah, a powerful Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Damascus, as Israel’s influence stretches toward the Euphrates.

f.g: God had promised Abraham’s descendants land as far as the Euphrates.

n: David captures a large force and disables most of the chariot horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots. Israel was not to trust in horses and chariots for its strength.

f.g: Hamstrung — cut the leg tendons so the horses could not be used in war.

n: When the Arameans of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, David defeats them too.

f.g: The leading city of Aram (Syria), northeast of Israel.

n: David stations garrisons in Damascus, and Syria pays him tribute. The narrator stresses the key point: the Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went

n: David brings the gold shields of Hadadezer’s officers back to Jerusalem as trophies.
He also takes a great deal of bronze from Hadadezer’s cities. Chronicles says Solomon later used this bronze to make temple furnishings.

f.g: In the KJV, “brass” usually means bronze, an alloy of copper and tin.

n: Toi, king of Hamath in Syria, hears of David’s victory over Hadadezer, his own enemy.

f.g: A city-state on the Orontes River in Syria, north of Zobah.

n: Toi sends his son with rich gifts to congratulate David and seek his friendship.

f.g: To greet him; to offer formal congratulations.

n: Instead of keeping the treasure for himself, David dedicates it to the Lord — a store that would help build the future temple.
The list of nations shows how broadly David’s kingdom now reached, and that all its plunder was devoted to God.
David wins fame by defeating a large army in the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea. Many manuscripts and 1 Chronicles read “Edomites” here instead of “Syrians,” which fits verse 14.

f.g: A valley near the Dead Sea, probably in the region of Edom.
In Hebrew, “Aram” (Syria) and “Edom” look very similar and were easily confused by copyists.

n: Edom also comes under David’s control. The refrain repeats that the Lord preserved David everywhere he went.

f.g: Descendants of Esau, Jacob’s twin; this fulfilled the prophecy that the elder would serve the younger.

n: Beyond conquest, David rules with justice and fairness for all his people — the true mark of a godly king.

f.g: Judgment = fair decisions; together the words mean doing what is right.

n: A list of David’s chief officials begins. Joab commands the army, and Jehoshaphat is the “recorder,” likely the royal herald or chief of state records.

f.g: Possibly the official who kept records and announced the king’s decisions.

n: Zadok and Ahimelech serve as priests, and Seraiah as royal secretary. Elsewhere Abiathar is the son of Ahimelech, so the names may have been reversed by a copyist.

f.g: A royal secretary who handled official documents and correspondence.

n: Benaiah commands David’s foreign bodyguard. David’s sons are called “chief rulers”; the Hebrew word usually means priests, perhaps meaning royal advisers or officials.

f.g: Probably Cretans and Philistines who served as David’s loyal royal guard.
Hebrew kohanim, normally “priests”; 1 Chronicles 18:17 says “chief about the king.”
